results.question: Compare the disk-induced tidal disruption-driven growth scenario for intermediate-mass black holes described in Rapid Growth of Intermediate-Mass Black Holes through Disk-induced Stellar Disruptions (arXiv:2609.03701v2) with the stellar clustering / bound-companion analysis methods used in Star cluster formation from turbulent clumps. V. Stellar clustering around massive stars (arXiv:2604.27382v2). Specifically: (1) What concrete dTDE mass supply rate and sensitivity to the disk outer radius does the Rapid Growth paper report? (2) What simulation/analysis capabilities from the Star cluster formation paper could be used to test or refine the assumptions about the stellar cusp and bound stellar populations feeding the IMBH in the Rapid Growth paper? Provide an explicit synthesis requiring supported facts from both papers.
results.reference_answer: (1) Rapid Growth of Intermediate-Mass Black Holes through Disk-induced Stellar Disruptions reports that disk-induced stellar disruptions can sustain stellar disruption rates of ~ (1–3) × 10^−3 M☉ yr^−1, and that extending the disk outer radius from R_out = R_sg to R_out = 3 R_sg produces only a slight decrease in the dTDE-driven mass supply (from ~8×10^−4 to ~6×10^−4 M☉ yr^−1), i.e., the overall dTDE rate is only weakly dependent on R_out (evidence: da98ceac0da2dfbc4cb8c97e; 41d12c9455789b742b18e36e). (2) The Star cluster formation from turbulent clumps. V. Stellar clustering around massive stars paper describes N-body models of gradual star cluster formation, post-processing to identify bound systems around massive stars, and constructing projected stellar density profiles to compare clustering predictions with observations (evidence: d26d531b97dd532abb0e07dc; 3f5057c15ab6fdac9f804821). Synthesis: By combining these capabilities, one could supply the Rapid Growth model with more realistic initial conditions for the stellar cusp and local bound-companion population: the clustering paper’s N-body simulations and bound-companion identification methods can quantify the number, radial distribution, and projected density profiles of stars near massive objects at specified cluster ages, which would directly test the Rapid Growth assumption about the available stellar reservoir for disk capture and inward migration. This addresses a limitation noted in Rapid Growth that their simulations model the local dynamical feeding mechanism but require galaxy-scale inputs about the formation and lifetime of gas-rich nuclear environments (da98ceac0da2dfbc4cb8c97e). Together, the Star cluster formation methods could refine the Rapid Growth dTDE supply estimates by providing empirically motivated stellar spatial and dynamical distributions for use in the disk-capture and migration prescriptions (evidence: da98ceac0da2dfbc4cb8c97e; d26d531b97dd532abb0e07dc).
results.answer:
The Rapid Growth paper reports a time-averaged dTDE stellar disruption rate of approximately (1–3) × 10^-3 M⊙ yr^-1 for IMBHs, stating this range as the sustained stellar disruption rate of the disk-induced mechanism. [1]

For three simulated IMBH masses the Rapid Growth paper reports measured dTDE mass-supply rates of 7.9 × 10^-4 M⊙ yr^-1 for M• = 3 × 10^3 M⊙, 7.8 × 10^-4 M⊙ yr^-1 for M• = 1 × 10^4 M⊙, and 2.6 × 10^-3 M⊙ yr^-1 for M• = 3 × 10^4 M⊙. [2]

The Rapid Growth paper reports adopting Rout = Rsg as the fiducial outer disk radius and shows that increasing the outer boundary to Rout = 3 Rsg produces a slight decrease in the dTDE rate from ~8 × 10^-4 to ~6 × 10^-4 M⊙ yr^-1 in the tested case. [1] [3]

The Rapid Growth paper explains the decrease when Rout is increased is attributed to the larger Rout raising the frequency of two-body and few-body encounters and stellar collisions within the disk, which perturb orbits and reduce disk-driven inward migration efficiency. [3]

The Star cluster formation paper uses direct N-body formation simulations post-processed to measure bound companions, reporting a snowballing algorithm to identify bound companions and producing the metric ⟨N_bound⟩ (average number of bound companions) around massive stars in different models. [4] [5]

The Star cluster formation paper provides companion-mass detection thresholds and comparative diagnostics: it varies companion-mass thresholds (M_comp = 0.01, 0.1, 1 M⊙) when computing ⟨N_bound⟩, and presents separation and mass-ratio distributions (including Figure 12) for bound companions around massive stars (≥ 16.0 M⊙) across models with different M_cl and Σ_cloud. [5] [6]

The Star cluster formation paper provides projected stellar density profiles and time/age diagnostics (e.g., metrics evaluated at cluster age t = 3.0 Myr and discussion of profile evolution with formation timescale ε_ff), which can be used to track cusp build-up and its time dependence. [7] [8]

Synthesis proposal: the Rapid Growth paper's sensitivity test showing a slight decrease in dTDE rate when Rout is increased to 3 Rsg (change ~8e-4 → ~6e-4 M⊙ yr^-1) could be constrained by using the Star cluster formation paper's parameter-space diagnostics—varying cluster compactness (M_cl, Σ_cloud) and formation timescale ε_ff and measuring resulting ⟨N_bound⟩ and companion separation distributions—to quantify how outer-cluster bound populations and encounter rates change with cluster structure and thereby affect the frequency of two-body/few-body encounters cited as the mechanism for the dTDE rate change. [3] [5] [6]

The Rapid Growth paper's reported sensitivity that increasing the disk outer radius from Rout = Rsg to Rout = 3 Rsg produces a slight decrease in the dTDE rate (from ≃ 8 × 10^-4 to ≃ 6 × 10^-4 M⊙ yr^-1) could be tested by measuring how the average number of bound companions ⟨N_bound⟩ (which the Star cluster formation paper computes) varies with cluster structural parameters, because ⟨N_bound⟩ quantifies the population of nearby bound stars that drive two-body and few-body encounter rates cited as the mechanism for the dTDE rate change. [3] [5]

The Star cluster formation paper's variation of companion-mass thresholds (M_comp = 0.01, 0.1, 1 M⊙) when computing ⟨N_bound⟩ can be applied to the Rapid Growth assumption about disk-driven capture and inward migration to test which companion-mass ranges contribute most to encounter-driven orbital perturbations that the Rapid Growth paper attributes to reducing inward migration efficiency when Rout is larger. [3] [5]

The Star cluster formation paper provides projected stellar density profiles evaluated at cluster age t = 3.0 Myr and discusses their time evolution with formation timescale ε_ff, so these projected-density diagnostics can be used to test the Rapid Growth paper's assumption about the presence and steepness of an inner stellar cusp feeding the disk (e.g., cusp build-up and replenishment timescales relevant to sustaining the reported dTDE rates). [1] [7]

The Star cluster formation paper's snowballing algorithm to identify bound companions (used to produce ⟨N_bound⟩ and separation/mass-ratio distributions) can be directly applied to N-body realizations of the Rapid Growth initial clusters to quantify the bound-subpopulation spatial and mass distributions that determine two-body/few-body encounter frequencies invoked by the Rapid Growth paper to explain the Rout → 3 Rsg dTDE rate decrease. [3] [4]

## 3.3. _Rate of disk-induced TDE_ 

In this subsection, we use the crossing of the inner accretion radius, _R_ dTDE = 10 _[−]_[4] pc, as the operational definition of a dTDE candidate. This radius connects the local orbital outcome of star–disk interactions to the global feeding rate of the IMBH. The disruption rate is not set only by the instantaneous number of stars inside the disk. It is controlled by a sequence of linked processes: stars must first be supplied to disk-crossing orbits by the collisional cluster, then dissipatively captured or driven inward by the disk, and finally avoid being scattered or collisionally removed before reaching _R_ dTDE.

In our fiducial model, we adopt _R_ out = _R_ sg, corresponding to the self-gravity radius of the disk. As shown in Figure 8, extending the outer boundary to _R_ out = 3 _R_ sg (red curve) does not significantly alter the rate of dTDEs compared with the fiducial case (blue curve), but instead leads to a slight decrease from _∼_ 8 _×_ 10 _[−]_[4] to _∼_ 6 _×_ 10 _[−]_[4] _M⊙_ yr _[−]_[1] . Although a larger _R_ out provides a larger population of stars that can interact with the disk, it also increases the frequency of two-body and few-body encounters, as well as stellar collisions within the disk. These additional dynamical interactions can perturb stellar orbits, increase their eccentricities and inclinations, and consequently reduce the efficiency of disk-driven inward migration. As a result, the overall dTDE rate remains only weakly dependent on the disk outer radius, suggesting that our conclusions are robust against reasonable variations in _R_ out. 

We further note that the structure of AGN accretion disks remains highly uncertain, with theoretical models spanning a wide range, from the canonical geometrically thin, thermal-pressure-dominated _α_ -disk to geometrically thicker configurations supported by radiation pressure, magnetic fields, or turbulence. Such geometrically thick disks are expected when these additional pressure components become dynamically important, for instance in radiation-pressure-dominated or strongly magnetized accretion flows. Variations in disk geometry can profoundly influence star–disk interactions. In particular, thick disks may suppress both the capture 

and subsequent inward migration of embedded stars, thereby significantly reducing the dTDE rate (Tomar et al. 2026).

disk interactions can act as a dissipative conveyor of stellar material: the disk captures stars from a threedimensional cluster, damps their orbits, and delivers them inward on a migration timescale. 

This mechanism is especially relevant for intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs). For _M•_ ≲ 10[5] _M⊙_ , the dTDE mass supply rate can exceed the Eddington-limited gas accretion rate, and may therefore dominate the early mass budget of the black hole. The problem is not simply whether an individual star can be captured by the disk; that can be estimated from local drag and migration timescales. The central question is whether a realistic collisional stellar cluster can maintain a continuous supply of stars to the disk after the innermost stars have been consumed. The answer depends on several coupled processes: the formation of a stellar cusp around the IMBH, two-body relaxation that refills the disk-crossing population, stochastic few-body encounters, mass segregation and stellar evolution, and physical collisions among stars that captured by the disk. These effects determine both the dTDE rate and the mass spectrum of the disrupted stars.

However, several caveats and limitations of this work warrant discussion. These limitations are particularly important for interpreting the high-redshift application: our simulations test the local dynamical feeding mechanism, while the formation and lifetime of the required gas-rich nuclear environment must be supplied by galaxy-scale gas inflow, star formation, and feedback. A deeper assessment of how disk-induced TDEs affect seed black hole growth in a cosmological setting will therefore be addressed using cosmological simulations in a companion paper (Wang Z. et al. in preparation), which shows that dTDEs can boost IMBH growth to _∼_ 10[5] _M⊙_ within several tens of millions of years, increasing the abundance of massive black holes at _z ∼_ 9–10 and partially alleviating the tension with JWST-discovered overmassive candidates.

_Choice of inner accretion radius._ —Due to computational limitations, we replace the tidal disruption radius _R_ t with a larger accretion radius _R_ dTDE. To assess the robustness of this treatment, we compare our fiducial model ( _R_ dTDE = 10 _[−]_[4] pc) with a run adopting a smaller value, _R_ dTDE = 5 _×_ 10 _[−]_[5] pc (green curve), in Figure 8. The resulting disruption rates are nearly identical, indicating that our results are insensitive to the specific choice of _R_ dTDE. This insensitivity is physically expected: once stars are captured by the accretion disk, they settle onto nearly circular orbits and rapidly migrate inward. After crossing _R_ dTDE, they continue migrating toward the central IMBH and typically reach the tidal disruption radius _R_ t within _∼_ 10[4] yr. Therefore, as long as _R_ dTDE is sufficiently small, the resulting stellar disruption rate converges and is insensitive to the exact choice of _R_ dTDE.

## 4. CONCLUSIONS AND DISCUSSIONS In this work, we investigate dTDEs as a stellar feeding channel for IMBHs embedded in gas-rich dense nuclear star clusters. By performing high-precision direct _N_ - body simulations with analytic prescriptions for star– disk interactions, we follow the coupled evolution of the stellar cusp, relaxation-driven replenishment, disk capture, inward migration, stellar mergers, and eventual accretion onto the central IMBH. We find that this process can sustain stellar disruption rates of _∼_ (1 _−_ 3) _×_ 10 _[−]_[3] _M⊙_ yr _[−]_[1] , significantly exceeding the Eddington accretion rate for black holes with _M• <_ 10[5] _M⊙_ . The main conclusion is therefore that disk-induced stellar disruptions can provide an efficient and dynamically sustained stellar mass supply to IMBHs in compact gasrich stellar systems. As a conditional application, this feeding channel can help grow _∼_ 10[3] _M⊙_ IMBHs toward ≳ 10[5] _M⊙_ if the required cluster and disk conditions are maintained. **==> picture [234 x 173] intentionally omitted <==** **----- Start of picture text -----**

retrieved_chunks.text: Due to the substantial computational cost of direct _N_ -body simulations, our current calculations are restricted to IMBH masses up to 3 _×_ 10[4] _M⊙_ , and we are unable to directly follow the dTDE evolution at larger black hole masses or on longer timescales. As a first step, we have performed simulations for only three discrete IMBH masses, from which we measure the˙ dTDE rates: _M_ dTDE = 7 _._ 9 _×_ 10 _[−]_[4] _M⊙_ yr _[−]_[1] for _M•_ = 3 _×_ 10[3] _M⊙_ , 7 _._ 8 _×_ 10 _[−]_[4] _M⊙_ yr _[−]_[1] for _M•_ = 1 _×_ 10[4] _M⊙_ , and 2 _._ 6 _×_ 10 _[−]_[3] _M⊙_ yr _[−]_[1] for _M•_ = 3 _×_ 10[4] _M⊙_ (see Figure 7). For IMBH masses within this range, we employ linear interpolation in the log _M•_ –log _M_[˙] dTDE plane based on these three data points. For black hole masses beyond 3 _×_ 10[4] _M⊙_ , we adopt a constant dTDE rate of 2 _._ 6 _×_ 10 _[−]_[4] _M⊙_ yr _[−]_[1] as a conservative extrapolation. This assumption is motivated by two physical considerations. First, the dTDE rate is not expected to increase indefinitely with black hole mass. As the black hole becomes more massive, the timescale for capturing stars through star–disk interactions becomes longer, preventing a continuous increase of the dTDE rate with black hole mass (Wang et al. 2024c). Second, the Eddington accretion rate of the surrounding gas disk increases with black hole mass, eventually making gas accretion the dominant growth channel and reducing the relative contribution of dTDEs (see Kennedy et al. 2016).

Theoretically, two-body relaxation predicts a powerlaw cusp _ρ ∝ r[−]_[1] _[.]_[75] for a relaxed stellar system around a massive black hole (Bahcall & Wolf 1976, 1977). Our results broadly follow this expectation, particularly for higher black hole masses. For _M•_ = 3 _×_ 10[3] _M⊙_ , the inner cusp remains relatively shallow due to the weaker gravitational influence and limited relaxation over 2 Myr. For the more massive central IMBH ( _M•_ = 3 _×_ 10[4] _M⊙_ ), the stellar density profile becomes significantly steeper, approaching _γ ∼−_ 1 _._ 75, consistent with the canonical Bahcall–Wolf solution. 

The two-body relaxation timescale at the influence radius of IMBH, _r_ h, is approximately 10 Myr, which exceeds the 2 Myr duration of the adiabatic growth phase adopted in our simulations. While this choice is primarily dictated by computational constraints, it is unlikely to significantly affect our inferred dTDE rates. Once the disk torque is switched on, the stellar distribution within _R_ out becomes progressively more cuspy as stars are efficiently captured and transported inward. Within this region, the local two-body relaxation timescale is below _∼_ 10[4] yr, whereas the characteristic inward migration timescale of stars through the disk is slightly longer than _∼_ 10[4] yr. Provided that the stellar replenishment rate in the vicinity of the disk, which is driven primarily by 

two-body relaxation and may be further enhanced by dynamical friction with gas clouds, exceeds the rate at which stars are consumed through inward migration, the dTDE rate can approach a quasi-steady state. This is consistent with the approximately constant dTDE rates observed over the duration of our simulations.

with the disk are then gradually captured onto nearcircular, coplanar orbits through the damping forces described above. Once captured, they migrate inward via Type I/II migration, eventually approaching the tidal disruption radius of the central IMBH. By evolving both stages in the same direct _N_ -body calculation, we can measure whether the dTDE rate is sustained by relaxation-driven replenishment rather than by the initially available inner stars alone. 

In our simulations, a star is considered accreted once its semi-major axis _a_ becomes smaller than _R_ dTDE. We adopt _R_ dTDE = 10 _[−]_[4] pc as our fiducial value, which is much larger than the actual physical tidal disruption radius _R_ t ( _∼_ 10 _[−]_[6] pc). This choice is primarily motivated by the computational cost associated with resolving the short orbital timescales near the central IMBH. For a representative IMBH mass of _M•_ = 10[4] _M⊙_ , the Keplerian orbital period at _R_ dTDE = 10 _[−]_[4] pc is approximately _P_ orb _≃_ 1 yr. Since our _N_ -body integration requires a timestep smaller than _P_ orb _/_ 32, resolving a significantly smaller accretion radius would substantially increase the computational cost. Therefore, we use this _R_ dTDE as a proxy for disruption, and this approximation can be justified by the fact that captured stars follow well-defined, deterministic migration trajectories(Just et al. 2012; Kennedy et al. 2016). Even for stars that are not yet fully embedded in the disk, once they cross _R_ dTDE, dynamical friction from the accretion disk will also drag them inward and lead to tidal disruption by the IMBH within _∼_ 10[4] yr (e.g., Wang et al. 2024c). For the same reason, extending our simulations to more massive IMBHs remains computationally challenging. In Section 4, we also perform a controlled run with _R_ dTDE = 5 _×_ 10 _[−]_[5] pc to verify that our results are insensitive to this choice.

## **2.2 Clustering around Massive Stars** 

We examine the stellar clustering around massive stars (≥ 8 _𝑀_ ⊙) formed in our simulations. To study the effect of cluster environment on such clustering, we divide these massive stars into three different subsets according to their location and boundedness. First, we determine stars that are bound to the star cluster using a snowballing algorithm developed in Farias & Tan (2023). Then, we refer bound massive stars in the central regions within 20% of the half-mass radius of their star cluster as _central stars_ . Similarly, massive stars beyond 20% of the half-mass radius which are in the outer regions of the star cluster are referred as _offset stars_ . Finally, massive stars that are unbound from the star cluster are referred to as _ejected stars_ . 

After dividing massive stars into subsets, we study the properties of bound and unbound companions around them. For this purpose, we have developed routines to identify bound companions around any given massive star. The routine works as follows: First, we identify the closest bound companion (a binary partner) to the massive star. Then, we replace the two stars with a center of mass particle. Next, we search for the next closest star that is bounded to this center of mass particle, hence forming a triple. If present, we replace the triple with its corresponding center of mass particle. Then, we search for the next closest bound companion. We perform this process iteratively to identify all the stars that are bound to the massive star. We start this search around the most massive star, identify its bound companions and tag them. Then, we move to the next most massive untagged star and search for its bound companions, ensuring there is no doublecounting of stars during this iterative process. This allows us to identify all the bound stars that are centered on independent primary massive stars within our star cluster.

## **4 DISCUSSION** 

In section 4.1, we discuss the effect of the star cluster environment on the bound systems around massive stars. In section 4.2, we discuss how projected stellar density profiles reflect the clustering of companions predicted by different massive star formation models. In section 4.3, we discuss the comparison of our bound companions with observed comparisons around O-stars. In section 4.4, we mention the caveats of our modeling and the scope for future improvements.

## _3.4.2 Comparison of companion properties_ 

Figure 12 shows the separation and mass-ratio of bound companions around all massive stars with masses ≥ 16 _._ 0 _𝑀_ ⊙ in our simulations. We compare them with observed companions around O-stars from the Southern Massive Stars at High Angular Resolution survey ( `SMASH+;` Tramper et al. 2025). This high angular resolution interferometric survey targeted nearby O-stars in the Southern hemisphere ( _𝛿<_ 0[◦] ) and identified companions around them. In addition to the comparison of full set of companions, we compare the different orders of companions separately, focusing on the binary and tertiary companions. We found M300L and M300H models to be the most comparable to their observations, because massive stars in higher _𝑀_ cl models have fewer companions (mostly singles or binaries, hence the smaller ⟨ _𝑁_ bound⟩). 

The survey had reported a relative scarcity of massive companions at large separations beyond 100 au, with few companions above _𝑞_ > 0.8 at such distances, which were mostly upper limits (Tramper et al. 2025). We observe a similar trend in our simulated companions in the M300 models, with large-distance companions having small mass ratios ( _𝑞<_ 0 _._ 4) beyond 1000 au. On the other hand, the `SMASH+` survey found close binary and tertiary companions within 10 au of some of these O-stars. In our simulations, we reproduce close binaries however, we lack close triple companions. Our closest triple companions are at separations of 100s of au. We discuss the implications of this lack of close triple companions in section 4.3. 

For M300L and M300H models, we ran two-sample KolmogorovSmirnov (K-S) test to check whether the similarity of the simulated and observed companion distributions for both separations and massratios. The results of the K-S test are presented in Table 4. We found that both M300L and M300H models were similar to the observed triple separations while only M300L was similar to the observed binary separations. For mass-ratios however, we did not find similarity between simulated and observed companions in these models.

## **5 CONCLUSIONS** 

Anosova J. P., 1986, Ap&SS, 124, 217 

- Appel S. M., et al., 2026, AJ, 172, 12 

In this paper, we studied the clustering of bound and unbound companions around massive stars inside gradually forming star clusters via “Turbulent Clump Core Accretion” (TCCA) by post-processing existing _𝑁_ −body simulations. In these simulations, star clusters are formed in different formation timescales ( _𝑡★_ ) parameterized by star formation efficiency per freefall time ( _𝜖_ ff), mass of star-forming clump ( _𝑀_ cl) and mass surface densities (Σcloud) of the parent cloud. 

We found that massive stars in the center of bound cluster gather more companions than massive stars that have been ejected from the cluster. We found that ejected stars are mostly single or in binaries. The number of companions is greater for massive stars in star clusters with lower stellar velocity dispersion and higher stellar densities. When we compared the clustering of companions around our massive stars with projected stellar density profiles, we found a good match to YSO profiles in the AFGL 5180 and G19.88-0.53 star-forming regions. Finally, we noted a lack of close triple companions around our simulated O-stars when compared to companions around O-stars in the `SMASH+` survey. Since these companions were not captured dynamically, they are likely formed via primordial routes like core or disk fragmentation. 

In the future, we aim to extend our gradual star cluster formation models with hydrodynamical coupling and an accurate treatment of primordial triples. We are also currently working on extending the analysis of dynamically gathered companions around primary stars across the full stellar mass spectrum.

## **2.1 Star Cluster Formation Simulations** 

In this work, we use the Turbulent Clump Core Accretion (TCCA) star cluster formation models developed by Farias et al. (2017, 2019); Farias & Tan (2023), where star clusters are formed inside magnetized, turbulent, gravitationally bound, and initially starless clumps within giant molecular clouds (GMCs). These consist of a suite of unique _𝑁_ -body simulations focused on accurately following stellar dynamics in the early stages of star cluster formation, i.e., where there is still ongoing formation of stars. These models assume individual stars and primordial binary stars form via stochastic core accretion with initial clump properties based on the Turbulent Core Accretion (TCA) model (McKee & Tan 2003). Farias et al. (2017) (hereafter, Paper I) presented the extreme case of instantaneous star cluster formation, where all stars are formed together at once and remaining gas is assumed to leave the system instantaneously according to a given global star formation efficiency (SFE, _𝜖_ ). Farias et al. (2019) and Farias & Tan (2023) (hereafter, Papers II and III, respectively) presented the case of gradual star cluster formation. In these simulations, we assume that a fraction ( _𝜖_ ) of the gas is gradually converted into stars while the remaining gas is also steadily removed from the system due to stellar feedback. This is modeled as a linear decrease of the gas reservoir (Equation 9, Paper III) until it reaches zero at the end of star formation, _𝑡★_ . The timescale over which this process occurs is set by the star formation efficiency per free-fall time, _𝜖_ ff, such that higher values of _𝜖_ ff result in shorter _𝑡★_ (see Paper III for details). The case of _𝜖_ ff = ∞ corresponds to the instantaneous case where all stars are formed at once, whereas the slowest case considered assumes _𝜖_ ff = 0.01. For this paper, we post-processed clusters formed from _𝑁_ -body models outlined in Paper III.

Massive stars are formed randomly in the star cluster, i.e., approximating the process of Turbulent Core Accretion in the limit of no primordial mass segregation of massive star formation. We perform an analysis of clustering of companions around these massive stars. We also compare with observations and massive stars formed by Competitive Accretion in `STARFORGE` simulations. In addition, the simulations involve 50% of systems being primordial binaries, but with no preference for massive stars to be favored as being in multiples. There are no primordial triples or higher-order multiples, so such systems must form dynamically during the evolution of the cluster. We track the formation of such bound systems of companions around massive stars to study the effect of star cluster environment on the dynamical capture of companions. This exploration yields benchmark statistics that can be used to compare the results of more sophisticated MHD + _𝑁_ -body simulations to be developed in future studies.

_Stellar clustering around massive stars_ 5 

profiles around these massive stars. In section 3.4, we compare these profiles and the properties of bound companions with observations. 

Before we begin, we note that typical, well-studied young starforming regions (ages ≲ 10 Myr) have a wide range of ages: 1-2 Myr (e.g., Ophiuchus; Wilking et al. 2008), 2-5 Myr (e.g., Taurus, Lupus, Chamaeleon I; Kenyon & Hartmann 1995; Alcalá et al. 2014; Luhman 2004) and 5-10 Myr (e.g., Upper Scorpius; Pecaut et al. 2012). One of the most notable is the Orion Nebula Cluster with stellar ages between ∼1 and ∼5 Myr (e.g., Da Rio et al. 2010; Reggiani et al. 2011; Fajrin et al. 2025). These age estimates have their own systematic uncertainties (e.g., Preibisch 2012), which are beyond the scope of our work. So, we have picked 3 Myr as a fiducial age for a typical young star-forming region. This adopted reference time can influence the trends we observe during our model comparisons at a given cluster age. Our different star clusters will have reached different stages at 3 Myr in terms of how advanced the star formation process is. However, this is also true for the observed systems; and unlike the simulations, we do not know which exact stage of the process a given star-forming region is currently in. So, in order to make a fair comparison between theoretical models in this work, we need to pick a fixed physical time (3 Myr). When we compare models with observations as in section 3.4, we generate the metrics at different ages to account for the uncertainty in our assumption for the typical age of the star-forming region.

## **4.2 Projected stellar density profiles and theories of massive star formation** 

Our TCCA models can be considered to represent a limiting case of the Turbulent Core Accretion (McKee & Tan 2003) model of massive star formation because massive stars are born randomly across the star cluster. They are not necessarily formed in regions of existing high stellar density, in which case they would form with many low-mass companions also forming around them and competing for gas accretion, as in models of Competitive Accretion (Bonnell et al. 2001; Grudić et al. 2022). We found that the TCCA model, which develops enhanced stellar multiplicity and clustering around massive stars dynamically after individual stars have formed, and Competitive Accretion models that have these features primordially as a crucial part of the massive star formation process, predict different shapes for projected stellar density profiles around massive stars. The Competitive Accretion models have more substructure due to the close low-mass companions. Hence, their projected stellar density profiles are steeper in comparison with the TCCA models, where star formation is more homogeneous. 

In addition, we noted the time evolution for projected stellar density profiles around massive stars in young forming star clusters. In TCCA, the projected stellar density profile builds up quickly over time as more stars are formed around the massive star. However, once the star cluster is formed and gas is dissipated away, the projected stellar density falls as the cluster expands. In star clusters that form quicker (for instance, higher _𝜖_ ff models), the projected stellar density profiles can build up and then fall to a baseline level quickly within the first few Myrs. This is true for Competitive Accretion as well, however the massive star takes time to grow in mass and gather enough companions, so the projected stellar density profile is still rising in the first few Myrs in those models.

## 3.2. _Orbital Inclination Decay Induced by Star–Disk Interactions_ 

After introducing the star–disk interactions at _t_ = 2 Myr, the accretion disk quickly imprints a strong dynamical signature on the surrounding stellar population. Figure 3 shows the distribution of stars in the semimajor axis versus orbital inclination plane at _t_ = 2 _._ 00, 2 _._ 08, 2 _._ 18, and 2 _._ 31 Myr. At the initial moment when the disk is activated ( _t_ = 2 Myr, top-left panel), the stellar orbits exhibit an isotropic inclination distribution, spanning uniformly from 0 to _π_ with a clear symmetry about _π/_ 2. This reflects the relaxed, nearly spherical configuration established during the adiabatic growth phase of the central IMBH. In this stage, the probability of finding stars with semi-major axes smaller than 0 _._ 001 pc is very low. 

Once the disk forces are turned on, a rapid transformation occurs in the inner region. At _t >_ 2 Myr, stars within the disk outer radius ( _R_ out _≈_ 0 _._ 003 pc) are efficiently captured onto near-coplanar orbits, forming a dense, coplanar structure with inclination _i ∼_ 0. This alignment is driven by repeated disk crossings, during which aerodynamic drag and gas dynamical friction (see equation (2)) efficiently dissipate the vertical component of stellar motion and progressively align the angular momentum vectors with the disk plane. In contrast, stars outside _R_ out remain largely unaffected and retain their initial isotropic inclination distribution. Meanwhile, stars embedded in the accretion disk migrate inward via density wave excitations and eventually reach the accretion radius _R_ dTDE.

claims.text: The Rapid Growth paper reports a time-averaged dTDE stellar disruption rate of approximately (1–3) × 10^-3 M⊙ yr^-1 for IMBHs, stating this range as the sustained stellar disruption rate of the disk-induced mechanism.

For three simulated IMBH masses the Rapid Growth paper reports measured dTDE mass-supply rates of 7.9 × 10^-4 M⊙ yr^-1 for M• = 3 × 10^3 M⊙, 7.8 × 10^-4 M⊙ yr^-1 for M• = 1 × 10^4 M⊙, and 2.6 × 10^-3 M⊙ yr^-1 for M• = 3 × 10^4 M⊙.

The Rapid Growth paper reports adopting Rout = Rsg as the fiducial outer disk radius and shows that increasing the outer boundary to Rout = 3 Rsg produces a slight decrease in the dTDE rate from ~8 × 10^-4 to ~6 × 10^-4 M⊙ yr^-1 in the tested case.

The Rapid Growth paper explains the decrease when Rout is increased is attributed to the larger Rout raising the frequency of two-body and few-body encounters and stellar collisions within the disk, which perturb orbits and reduce disk-driven inward migration efficiency.

The Star cluster formation paper uses direct N-body formation simulations post-processed to measure bound companions, reporting a snowballing algorithm to identify bound companions and producing the metric ⟨N_bound⟩ (average number of bound companions) around massive stars in different models.

The Star cluster formation paper provides companion-mass detection thresholds and comparative diagnostics: it varies companion-mass thresholds (M_comp = 0.01, 0.1, 1 M⊙) when computing ⟨N_bound⟩, and presents separation and mass-ratio distributions (including Figure 12) for bound companions around massive stars (≥ 16.0 M⊙) across models with different M_cl and Σ_cloud.

The Star cluster formation paper provides projected stellar density profiles and time/age diagnostics (e.g., metrics evaluated at cluster age t = 3.0 Myr and discussion of profile evolution with formation timescale ε_ff), which can be used to track cusp build-up and its time dependence.

Synthesis proposal: the Rapid Growth paper's sensitivity test showing a slight decrease in dTDE rate when Rout is increased to 3 Rsg (change ~8e-4 → ~6e-4 M⊙ yr^-1) could be constrained by using the Star cluster formation paper's parameter-space diagnostics—varying cluster compactness (M_cl, Σ_cloud) and formation timescale ε_ff and measuring resulting ⟨N_bound⟩ and companion separation distributions—to quantify how outer-cluster bound populations and encounter rates change with cluster structure and thereby affect the frequency of two-body/few-body encounters cited as the mechanism for the dTDE rate change.

The Rapid Growth paper's reported sensitivity that increasing the disk outer radius from Rout = Rsg to Rout = 3 Rsg produces a slight decrease in the dTDE rate (from ≃ 8 × 10^-4 to ≃ 6 × 10^-4 M⊙ yr^-1) could be tested by measuring how the average number of bound companions ⟨N_bound⟩ (which the Star cluster formation paper computes) varies with cluster structural parameters, because ⟨N_bound⟩ quantifies the population of nearby bound stars that drive two-body and few-body encounter rates cited as the mechanism for the dTDE rate change.

The Star cluster formation paper's variation of companion-mass thresholds (M_comp = 0.01, 0.1, 1 M⊙) when computing ⟨N_bound⟩ can be applied to the Rapid Growth assumption about disk-driven capture and inward migration to test which companion-mass ranges contribute most to encounter-driven orbital perturbations that the Rapid Growth paper attributes to reducing inward migration efficiency when Rout is larger.

The Star cluster formation paper provides projected stellar density profiles evaluated at cluster age t = 3.0 Myr and discusses their time evolution with formation timescale ε_ff, so these projected-density diagnostics can be used to test the Rapid Growth paper's assumption about the presence and steepness of an inner stellar cusp feeding the disk (e.g., cusp build-up and replenishment timescales relevant to sustaining the reported dTDE rates).

The Star cluster formation paper's snowballing algorithm to identify bound companions (used to produce ⟨N_bound⟩ and separation/mass-ratio distributions) can be directly applied to N-body realizations of the Rapid Growth initial clusters to quantify the bound-subpopulation spatial and mass distributions that determine two-body/few-body encounter frequencies invoked by the Rapid Growth paper to explain the Rout → 3 Rsg dTDE rate decrease.

answer_quotes: The Star cluster formation paper's snowballing algorithm to identify bound companions (used to produce ⟨N_bound⟩ and separation/mass-ratio distributions) can be directly applied to N-body realizations of the Rapid Growth initial clusters to quantify the bound-subpopulation spatial and mass distributions that determine two-body/few-body encounter frequencies invoked by the Rapid Growth paper to explain the Rout → 3 Rsg dTDE rate decrease.
